description:
A half-finished API migration across a 37-file service: Store.put() became the all-or-nothing Store.put_many(). Six files changed, thirty-one untouched. The untouched files carry the symbol names the live trace chased - _resolve, compare_digest, SKIP LOCKED, SecretStr, mkdtemp, is_cancelled - so with the scope jail off they are the temptation surface, and with it on they are refusals. Neither defect is visible in one file; both need the contract in store/base.py held against a call site.

This is the BUDGET fixture, and its history is the point. It was built to reproduce budget_breach:iterations and never did - the agent batches all six reads into one turn, so width buys no iterations. What it reproduced instead was worse: store/codec.py is 103KB, read_file head-truncated it to the first 60KB, and that 60KB sat past every cache breakpoint and was re-sent uncached on every turn - 205,513 tokens against a 200,000 cap. The run still reported `published`, because every budget check lived in execute_tools and the turn that emits findings calls no tools. That missing check is fixed in agent/nodes.py:_spent.

expect_state is `published` because the failure mode is gone, not because it was waived. Phase 3 replaced head-truncation with hunk-centred reads: the diff touches codec.py at lines 2724-2741, so read_file now returns about 3,641 chars around the change instead of 61,440 chars of generated lookup table that did not even contain the changed code. The same fixture now finishes at roughly 2,694 tokens - about 1.3% of the cap - and publishes.

It remains the regression fixture for budget and read efficiency, which is why codec.py must stay at 103KB. If hunk-centred reads regress to head-truncation, or the rolling cache breakpoint stops covering tool results, this fixture goes back over the 200,000-token cap - and because _spent is now in place it will degrade loudly instead of reporting success. Correctness is not the signal here: tp 2 is expected either way, and precision alone said nothing about the run being over budget.
